(1) Nine of the twelve timing workloads are host-launch bound: profiled device task duration for selu_-timing-0 (fp16 [1024]) is 1.65 us against a 13.16 us walltime, and a target-side host-cost probe measured the candidate's per-call host path at 12.17 us versus 11.5 us for the PyTorch reference wrapper shape and 9.2 us for the bare compiled-launcher floor. (2) The three large workloads are device bound and dominated by the number of MTE transfers rather than by bytes or program count: the candidate runs fp16 [4096,4096] at 45.6 us (vector 27.2 us), bf16 at 83.2 us (vector 56.7 us) and fp32 at 82.6 us (vector 46.3 us); a target probe shows a pure copy kernel at BLOCK 16384 costs 40.2 us versus 78.1 us at BLOCK 8192 for the same bytes, and 2 tiles per program at BLOCK 8192 costs 77.3 us, so device time tracks transfer count, and the fp32-domain math needs three full-width UB tiles live, which caps BLOCK at 8192 for bf16/fp32 (every BLOCK 16384 variant fails to compile with ub overflow, including enable_ubuf_saving and a tightened fma form).

conclusion.root_cause: The bf16 root cause is confirmed and was fixed as predicted: bf16 was running fp32-domain math, which needs three live full-width UB tiles and therefore caps BLOCK at 8192, doubling the MTE transfer count relative to fp16 at BLOCK 16384; the fp16-width bf16 branch compiles at 16384 and delivers the predicted 63.5 us. The aggregate regression has a different, unrelated cause: bilateral machine-level drift of about 12% on the host-bound small workloads between the round-2 and round-3 measurements, which the retest quantified and which no code change in this round could have produced.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: The frozen expectation was that halving the bf16 transfer count would move selu_-timing-7 from 0.71 toward 0.90, and the workload-level evidence matched exactly: 83.310 -> 63.477 us, speedup 0.710 -> 0.932, versus the 64.45 us that the pre-round target probe predicted, with correctness unchanged (0 bad elements; bf16 correctness cases still 1.0 matched ratio, max rel err 0.044). The aggregate nevertheless fell from 0.8839 to 0.8670 because the nine small workloads, whose kernels and host path are byte-identical to round 2 and which this change cannot affect, all moved +1.5 to +2.0 us together with their own reference latencies. A full-suite retest confirmed the drift was bilateral and not the candidate: reference latencies returned to 10.46-11.75 us (from 11.94-13.30) and candidate latencies to 11.64-13.66 us, giving a remeasured geo_mean of 0.8727 with timing-7 (63.472 us) and timing-11 (82.682 us) unchanged within 0.1%. So the device change delivered its predicted 31% on timing-7, while the headline metric moved the opposite way purely through measurement drift on the host-bound majority; the round is not an improvement on the ledger even though its kernel is strictly better on the one workload it targets.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Re-establish the verified bf16 narrowing (it is a real 83.3 -> 63.5 us device win on selu_-timing-7 and has no effect on any other dtype, since the bf16 branch is compile-time eliminated elsewhere) and, in the same submission, recover the remaining host-side slack measured on target by dropping the extra Python frame and the unused tensor argument on the launcher call, then verify the combined form under the retest path if the two sides drift again.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A geo_mean comparison across rounds on this shared card is only meaningful if both sides moved together: here the reference latencies for the nine small workloads swung 11.7 -> 12.5 -> 11.2 us mean across three measurements of the same code, which is larger than any host-path change made so far. Round-to-round comparisons therefore need the retest path or a per-workload device-task measurement before concluding that a candidate regressed.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 2 exhausted the host-launch lever; round 3 moved to the device/transfer-count regime and its mechanism was verified per workload, but the ledger decision is dominated by drift on the other twelve-twelfths of the suite. Strategy changes accordingly: subsequent rounds must pair a verified device win with same-state verification (retest) rather than trusting a single cross-round aggregate.

plan.strategy: Vectorize the Philox device path and remove launch-bound host overhead while repairing the two independent-gate semantic defects (dtype-exact lower clamp, contiguous output for strided input).
plan.code_changes: 1) Replaced tl.philox with a manual vectorized Philox4x32-10 in uint32 arithmetic (16-bit split multiply-high, masked low-word reconstruction) in the same counter/key layout as the seed. 2) Replaced the seed's in-kernel fp32 round-trip bound computation with host-computed, dtype-exact clamp bounds (smallest representable value >= from_, largest < to) passed as two float scalars, then clamped with min/max after the store conversion. 3) Output allocated contiguous via torch.empty(shape, dtype, device) so a strided self is handled. 4) Host RNG state via generator.initial_seed()/get_offset()/set_offset() advancing exactly grid*BLOCK counters, replacing philox_backend_seed_offset. 5) BLOCK = clamp(next_pow2(n/160), 64, 4096) with the heuristics decorator removed, so grid >= ~40 programs for large tensors.
plan.hypothesis: The seed device kernel is dominated by a scalarised tl.philox lowering (~350 us for one 1024-lane program, ~7x350 us for 1M elements) and the per-call host cost by the generator state ByteTensor round-trip; replacing both and fixing the two independent-gate semantic defects (missing nearest-dtype lower clamp, stride-unsafe output allocation) should cut small-case latency from ~0.35 ms toward ~0.13 ms and large-case latency from ~2.45 ms toward ~0.13 ms.

expected_effect.mechanism: The seed spends ~0.25 us per lane inside a scalarised tl.philox (351 us for a single 1024-lane program) plus ~27 us of host RNG-state fetch and a stride-unsafe allocation; a vectorized Philox removes the device cost and the lean state API plus better-shaped blocks cut the launch-bound floor.

conclusion.root_cause: Two costs dominated the seed: (1) tl.philox is scalarised on this backend at ~0.25 us per lane (351 us for a single 1024-lane program; 1M elements = 7 waves x 350 us because only 40 vector cores process 256 programs), and (2) per-call host work, chiefly the generator state ByteTensor round-trip (27.1 us vs 0.90 us for initial_seed/get_offset/set_offset) plus a stride-unsafe empty_like. Replacing tl.philox with a vectorised manual Philox4x32-10 (identical to Random123's key schedule, 16-bit split multiply-high), taking the RNG offset through the lean API, allocating a contiguous output and choosing BLOCK so that ~40+ programs exist removed both, leaving only the ~70 us Triton launch overhead.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation was a drop from ~0.35 ms to ~0.13 ms on the launch-bound cases and from ~2.45 ms to ~0.13 ms on the 1M cases; observed 0.111-0.116 ms and 0.116-0.120 ms, i.e. slightly better than predicted, and geo_mean rose 0.1520 -> 0.8924 (5.87x). Every case now sits 6-20 us above the reference call (0.093-0.115 ms), and latency is flat across 1024/65536/1048576 elements, so the remainder is per-call host work, dominated by the ~70 us Triton metacall. Round 1 measured that same launch floor at 58-64 us for a store-only kernel, which bounds the achievable gain from a naked launcher at roughly +50-60% on this metric.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the remaining ~70 us per-call Triton Python launch overhead: cache the CompiledKernel returned by the first launch and re-enter it through the backend launcher entry point (the probe reported it takes 18 arguments for this 8-argument kernel), keeping the plain kernel[grid](...) path as a fallback, so the launch-bound cases approach the reference's ~0.10 ms.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Two independent-gate defects were invisible to the KG contract and had to be checked directly: (a) a float32 draw in [from, to) rounds below from in low precision, so the lower bound also needs a nearest-dtype clamp; (b) torch.empty_like on a strided self yields a non-contiguous buffer that a flat store pattern leaves partly uninitialised. Probe 4 also showed that an in-kernel comparison written as from_.to(DT).to(tl.float32) < from_ is folded to an identity, silently disabling the clamp; computing the bounds on the host removed that class of failure. The 16-bit multiply-high alternative was sound only after the CPU identity check exposed a wrong low-word reconstruction.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 established a flat 0.35 ms floor across 1024/65536 elements with 2.41-2.45 ms at 1M, which excluded the store path and dtype conversion as causes. Bounded target probes then separated the device cost (scalarised tl.philox, 0.25 us/lane) from the host cost (state tensor round-trip) and from the Triton launch floor (~60 us for any kernel), so the rewrite targeted the RNG implementation and the wrapper rather than tiles or unroll factors.

plan.strategy: Replace the one-tile-per-program launch for large inputs with a single-wave persistent streaming launch capped by the device's vector-core count.
plan.code_changes: Added _rad2deg_stream_kernel: pid strides over tiles by BLOCK * tl.num_programs(0) inside a tl.range loop, so one program covers a strip of tiles. Added _num_vec_core (queried from driver.active.utils.get_device_properties -> num_vectorcore = 40) and _stream_grid(), which launches min(ceil(n/BLOCK), num_vectorcore) programs. Inputs above 131072 elements now use this kernel with BLOCK=16384; the <=131072 paths and the strided path are byte-identical to round 1. Launcher cache is keyed by (path, dtype, data_ptr & 15) with the tile size stored in the entry.
plan.hypothesis: At 4096x4096 the candidate's device time is dominated by the number of programs rather than by bytes: 16.7M/32768 gives 512 programs = 12.8 sequential waves, and the candidate's fp16 and fp32 times are nearly dtype-independent (27.8us vs 31.0us for twice the bytes) while the oracle's scale with bytes. Collapsing the launch to one wave of streaming programs should cut the fp16/bf16 cases most and leave the nine host-bound small/medium cases untouched.

expected_effect.mechanism: Replacing 512 one-tile programs (12.8 sequential waves over 40 vector cores, each wave paying a full program prologue plus a load-wait-compute-store-drain cycle) with a single wave of <=40 streaming programs that multi-buffer consecutive tiles inside one program removes the per-program dispatch/drain cost that the paired profile attributes to the aiv_mte2_ratio of 0.339 versus the oracle's 0.935.

conclusion.root_cause: The hypothesis that the three 4096x4096 workloads are limited by per-program dispatch cost is refuted. The streaming kernel launched 40 programs (one wave) of 16384-element tiles instead of 512 programs of 32768-element tiles, and the fp16/bf16 cases became slower, while the fp32 case also degraded. Halving the tile size halved the bytes moved per transport step, so the loop gained nothing from having one program per core and lost transport efficiency; the dominant cost is bytes per transport step, not the number of programs.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expected effect: geomean increase driven by the three 4096x4096 workloads. Observed: geomean 0.78141 versus 0.80897 at round 1 (is_new_best false). The two cleanly comparable workloads, whose reference latency was unchanged in this run (rad2deg_-timing-3 reference 17.033->17.060us, rad2deg_-timing-7 19.132->19.193us), moved the wrong way: timing-3 27.837->30.205us (speedup 0.612->0.565) and timing-7 29.923->32.345us (0.639->0.593), i.e. about 8% slower. The rest of the run was degraded by environment noise rather than by the change: rad2deg_-timing-8/9/10 run byte-identical code to round 1 (n=1024/65536/1048576 use the untouched contiguous path) yet moved 13.79/13.49/13.84->16.13/16.32/15.30us, and the rad2deg_-timing-11 reference itself rose 28.79->39.67us. Interpretation: per-program dispatch/drain overhead was not the limiter; transport efficiency follows bytes per transport step, and replacing a 32768-element tile by a 16384-element tile inside a loop cut the per-step transport size in half, which cost more than the saved program count. The round-1 kernel already keeps every tile at 64KB (fp16) / 128KB (fp32), the largest that fits the 192KB UB budget.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Abandon program-count reduction for the large path and revert to the round-1 one-tile-per-program kernel (BLOCK=32768). Spend the next round on the nine host-issue-bound small/medium workloads instead: quantify the pure raw-launcher cost versus the Python bookkeeping around it with a bounded probe, then cut the per-call Python work (single cached entry per (dtype, alignment), no size-class branching, precomputed grid expression) so the fixed cost moves from 13.5-14.5us toward the 11.6-12.0us oracle floor.

The next hypothesis moves to the other bottleneck measured in round 1: the fixed per-call host cost of the nine small/medium workloads, where the candidate is at 13.5-14.5us against an 11.6-12.0us oracle floor and the device kernel is fully hidden.

plan.strategy: Expose the large 2-byte in-place loop as a two-pointer operation so the compiler can keep consecutive tiles in flight.
plan.code_changes: Added _rad2deg_stream_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK) which strides tiles by BLOCK * tl.num_programs(0) inside a tl.range loop and stores through y_ptr. For inputs above 131072 elements whose element size is 2 bytes, the cold path binds this kernel with BLOCK=16384 and a grid of min(ceil(n/BLOCK), num_vectorcore), passing the same buffer as both pointer arguments; every other case (2-byte and 4-byte inputs <=131072, all 4-byte large inputs) keeps the round-3 contiguous kernel unchanged. The small-input hot path was left byte-identical, and the 4-byte large path still uses one tile of 32768 per program.
plan.hypothesis: rad2deg_-timing-3 and rad2deg_-timing-7 are stuck near 0.61-0.64 while rad2deg_-timing-11 (fp32) reaches 0.93, and round 2 showed their per-byte transport cost is unchanged by program count or tile size, so they are limited by transport/arithmetic overlap rather than by tiling. Triton cannot overlap an in-place loop because the store and the following load share one base pointer. Giving the compiler two pointer arguments over the same storage should restore that overlap for 2-byte data without touching the fp32 case or any host-bound case.

expected_effect.mechanism: With one pointer serving as both load and store source the next iteration's load must be assumed to alias the previous iteration's store, so tiles are serialised and the transport engine idles; two distinct pointer arguments let consecutive tiles be in flight together, which is the overlap the oracle's 0.935 MTE2-active profile exhibits against this kernel's 0.339.

conclusion.root_cause: Passing the in-place buffer as two distinct pointer arguments let the compiler stop serialising consecutive tiles, which removed the transport idle time on the two 2-byte 4096x4096 workloads and confirmed that their deficit was lack of load/store overlap, not tiling, program count, masking, or arithmetic precision. The round's aggregate regression is entirely a shared host-side environment shift of ~3.5us that hit workloads whose code is byte-identical to round 3, so the ledger's cross-run geomean comparison rejects an otherwise correct device optimisation.
